concepts.name: Argument from beauty
concepts.note: Infers a divine creator from objective, non-instrumental beauty in nature and human aesthetic experience.

concepts.name: Aesthetic argument
concepts.note: Alternative name for the argument from beauty.

concepts.name: Objective beauty
concepts.note: Beauty treated as a real, mind-independent property rather than mere preference.

concepts.name: Disinterested pleasure
concepts.note: Aesthetic enjoyment experienced independently of practical use or possession.

concepts.name: Form of Beauty
concepts.note: Plato’s eternal reality unifying beautiful particulars and guiding ascent to higher knowledge.

concepts.name: Ladder of love
concepts.note: Diotima’s progression from bodily beauty toward the singular Form of Beauty.

concepts.name: Beauty as transcendental
concepts.note: Scholastic property coextensive with being alongside unity, truth, and goodness.

concepts.name: Integritas
concepts.note: Wholeness identified as one formal condition of beauty.

concepts.name: Proportio
concepts.note: Due proportion identified as one formal condition of beauty.

concepts.name: Claritas
concepts.note: Clarity or radiance identified as one formal condition of beauty.

concepts.name: Uniformity amidst variety
concepts.note: Hutcheson’s account of beauty as perceived regularity combined with diversity.

axioms.name: Objective beauty exists
axioms.note: The argument assumes beauty is a genuine property discernible beyond individual preference.

axioms.name: Naturalism inadequately explains beauty
axioms.note: Evolutionary and physical processes allegedly do not explain gratuitous aesthetic qualities.

principles.name: Modus tollens
principles.note: The argument reasons that denying God would undermine objective beauty, which exists.

principles.name: Inference to the best explanation
principles.note: Theism is presented as the superior explanation of pervasive, non-utilitarian beauty.

methods.name: Bayesian assessment
methods.note: Swinburne treats beauty as evidence that raises the probability of theism.

theories.name: Divinity Theory
theories.note: Pruss’s account explains beauty as creatures reflecting and participating in divine perfection.

frameworks.name: Teleological reasoning
frameworks.note: The broader reasoning pattern infers intentional agency from features of the world.

coined_terms.name: Axiology
coined_terms.note: Paul Lapie introduced the term in 1902 for the systematic study of value.

concepts.name: Value
concepts.note: The subject of axiology, concerning what makes things worthy, good, or desirable.

concepts.name: Intrinsic value
concepts.note: Worth possessed for its own sake, independently of consequences.

concepts.name: Instrumental value
concepts.note: Worth derived from serving as a means to an intrinsically valuable end.

concepts.name: Positive value
concepts.note: Value classified as good, desirable, or beneficial.

concepts.name: Negative value
concepts.note: Value classified as bad, undesirable, or harmful.

concepts.name: Absolute value
concepts.note: Value treated as universal and independent of context.

concepts.name: Relative value
concepts.note: Value dependent on circumstances, culture, or individual perspective.

concepts.name: Personal values
concepts.note: Values reflecting individual preferences and character commitments.

concepts.name: Social values
concepts.note: Values governing interaction and communal harmony.

concepts.name: Cultural values
concepts.note: Collective traditions and norms shaping group identity.

concepts.name: Spiritual values
concepts.note: Values emphasizing transcendence, meaning, and sacred connection.

concepts.name: Value realism
concepts.note: The view that values exist objectively and independently of human attitudes.

concepts.name: Value anti-realism
concepts.note: The view that values depend on attitudes, emotions, or social construction.

concepts.name: Moral realism
concepts.note: The position that moral facts are objective and mind-independent.

concepts.name: Subjectivism
concepts.note: The position that values are grounded in personal preferences or desires.

concepts.name: Emotivism
concepts.note: The view that value judgments express approval or disapproval.

concepts.name: Error theory
concepts.note: Mackie’s view that ordinary value claims are systematically false.

concepts.name: Value pluralism
concepts.note: The view that distinct intrinsic values may be equally valid and incomparable.

concepts.name: Universals
concepts.note: Values understood as abstract properties shared across instances.

concepts.name: Tropes
concepts.note: Values understood as particularized property instances attached to specific bearers.

concepts.name: Dispositions
concepts.note: Values understood as capacities to produce responses or relations.

axioms.name: Value axioms
axioms.note: Foundational value claims treated by foundationalism as self-evident supports for further judgments.

principles.name: Principle of organic unities
principles.note: Moore’s view that a whole’s value may differ from the sum of its parts.

principles.name: Supervenience
principles.note: Value properties are held to depend necessarily on non-evaluative facts.

methods.name: Isolation test
methods.note: Moore’s method asks whether a state would remain valuable in complete isolation.

theories.name: Consequentialism
theories.note: Moral value is assessed by the goodness of outcomes.

theories.name: Deontology
theories.note: Moral value is grounded in adherence to duties or rules.

theories.name: Virtue ethics
theories.note: Moral value is located in excellent character and human flourishing.

theories.name: Formalism
theories.note: Artistic value resides in formal properties such as composition and structure.

theories.name: Expressionism
theories.note: Artistic value arises from conveying emotional or subjective states.

theories.name: Institutional theory of art
theories.note: Art status and aesthetic worth are conferred by artworld conventions.

theories.name: Non-naturalism
theories.note: Goodness is treated as a simple, irreducible, non-natural property.

frameworks.name: Max Scheler’s hierarchy of values
frameworks.note: Ranks values from sensual and vital through spiritual to holy values.

frameworks.name: Deep ecology
frameworks.note: Attributes inherent value to living beings and ecosystems beyond human utility.

frameworks.name: Maslow’s hierarchy of needs
frameworks.note: Arranges human needs from physiological necessities toward self-actualization.

concepts.name: Bad faith
concepts.note: Self-deception through which a person denies freedom and responsibility by treating themselves as determined.

concepts.name: Mauvaise foi
concepts.note: French term for bad faith.

concepts.name: Authenticity
concepts.note: Lucidly owning freedom, projects, and responsibility rather than evading them.

concepts.name: Facticity
concepts.note: The given bodily, historical, social, and situational conditions of existence.

concepts.name: Transcendence
concepts.note: Consciousness’s capacity to surpass given circumstances through future possibilities.

concepts.name: Anguish
concepts.note: Distress arising from awareness of radical freedom and responsibility.

concepts.name: Nausea
concepts.note: Existential unease associated with contingency and ungrounded existence.

concepts.name: For-itself
concepts.note: Consciousness as negation, incompleteness, freedom, and transcendence.

concepts.name: In-itself
concepts.note: Object-like being characterized by inertness, positivity, and determination.

concepts.name: Lie to oneself
concepts.note: Bad faith’s paradoxical self-deception within a unified consciousness.

concepts.name: Being-for-others
concepts.note: Existence shaped through relation to other people and their gaze.

principles.name: Condemned to be free
principles.note: Sartre’s claim that humans cannot escape the necessity of choosing.

principles.name: Freedom entails responsibility
principles.note: Agency and accountability remain linked even under significant constraints.

theories.name: Existential phenomenology
theories.note: Analyzes conscious existence through freedom, facticity, transcendence, and lived experience.

theories.name: Ontological duality of for-itself and in-itself
theories.note: Sartre’s distinction between conscious freedom and object-like being.

frameworks.name: Beauvoir’s ethics of ambiguity
frameworks.note: Extends bad faith into relational ethics by requiring reciprocal recognition of freedom.

concepts.name: Bounded rationality
concepts.note: Decision-making constrained by limited information, time, and cognitive capacity.

concepts.name: Satisficing
concepts.note: Selecting an acceptable option rather than exhaustively maximizing utility.

concepts.name: Loss aversion
concepts.note: Losses typically weigh more heavily than equivalent gains.

concepts.name: Reference point
concepts.note: Outcomes are evaluated relative to a psychologically meaningful baseline.

concepts.name: Anchoring
concepts.note: Initial values disproportionately influence later judgments.

concepts.name: Overconfidence
concepts.note: Excessive confidence in one’s judgments or abilities.

concepts.name: Present bias
concepts.note: Immediate outcomes receive disproportionate weight over future outcomes.

concepts.name: Framing effect
concepts.note: Equivalent information produces different choices when presented differently.

concepts.name: Mental accounting
concepts.note: People segregate resources into subjective accounts based on source or purpose.

concepts.name: Endowment effect
concepts.note: Ownership increases the value people assign to an item.

concepts.name: Animal spirits
concepts.note: Keynesian spontaneous optimism or pessimism influencing investment.

concepts.name: Conspicuous consumption
concepts.note: Status-driven spending motivated by display and emulation.

concepts.name: Recognition heuristic
concepts.note: Choosing a familiar option when recognition is informative.

concepts.name: Social preferences
concepts.note: Preferences incorporating fairness, reciprocity, and concern for others.

concepts.name: Present value
concepts.note: Subjective value of delayed rewards under intertemporal choice.

principles.name: Money fungibility
principles.note: The standard economic principle that money’s value should not depend on its account or source.

principles.name: Descriptive invariance
principles.note: Rational choice models require equivalent descriptions not to change preferences.

methods.name: Heuristics
methods.note: Cognitive shortcuts enabling efficient judgment under limited information.

methods.name: Nudge
methods.note: A choice-design intervention guiding behavior without eliminating alternatives.

methods.name: Choice architecture
methods.note: Designing decision contexts to influence choices through defaults and presentation.

theories.name: Prospect theory
theories.note: Describes risk decisions using reference points, loss aversion, and nonlinear probability weighting.

theories.name: Hyperbolic discounting
theories.note: Models declining subjective value of rewards as delay increases.

theories.name: Behavioral game theory
theories.note: Models strategic interaction using bounded cognition and social preferences.

theories.name: Expected utility theory
theories.note: Normative benchmark assuming rational evaluation of probabilities and utilities.

frameworks.name: Adaptive toolbox
frameworks.note: Gigerenzer’s framework of simple heuristics suited to particular environments.

frameworks.name: Libertarian paternalism
frameworks.note: Guides choices toward welfare while preserving freedom to choose.

concepts.name: Broadening effect
concepts.note: Positive emotions temporarily expand attention, cognition, and possible actions.

concepts.name: Building effect
concepts.note: Repeated positive emotions accumulate enduring physical, intellectual, social, and psychological resources.

concepts.name: Upward spiral
concepts.note: Positive emotion and resource accumulation reinforce one another over time.

concepts.name: Thought-action repertoire
concepts.note: The range of thoughts and behaviors immediately available to a person.

concepts.name: Joy
concepts.note: Positive emotion associated with play, creativity, and skill development.

concepts.name: Interest
concepts.note: Positive emotion motivating exploration and acquisition of knowledge.

concepts.name: Contentment
concepts.note: Positive emotion supporting savoring and reflective integration.

concepts.name: Love
concepts.note: Positive emotion that builds durable social bonds.

concepts.name: Personal resources
concepts.note: Enduring capacities such as resilience, coping skills, and social support.

principles.name: Positive emotions broaden cognition
principles.note: Positive emotions widen thought-action repertoires beyond immediate survival responses.

principles.name: Positive emotions build resources
principles.note: Temporary broadened states can accumulate lasting adaptive resources.

principles.name: Undoing hypothesis
principles.note: Positive emotions can accelerate cardiovascular recovery after negative arousal.

methods.name: Best possible self writing
methods.note: Participants envision and describe an ideal future self to elicit positive emotion.

methods.name: Loving-kindness meditation
methods.note: Practice directing warmth and compassion toward oneself and others.

methods.name: Gratitude practice
methods.note: Journaling or reflection used to evoke appreciation and positive affect.

theories.name: Broaden-and-build theory
theories.note: Fredrickson’s theory links positive emotions with expanded cognition and lasting resources.

frameworks.name: Belong, Broaden, and Build
frameworks.note: Developmental framework adding belonging to positive emotion’s broadening and resource-building functions.

coined_terms.name: Codependency
coined_terms.note: Term emerging from co-alcoholism discussions and broadened to dysfunctional relational dependence.

concepts.name: Codependency
concepts.note: Excessive reliance involving self-sacrifice, caretaking, enabling, and poor boundaries.

concepts.name: Savior complex
concepts.note: Compulsion to rescue others as a source of self-worth.

concepts.name: Compulsive helping
concepts.note: Excessive uncontrollable assistance that neglects one’s own needs.

concepts.name: Enabling
concepts.note: Actions that support another person’s harmful or dysfunctional behavior.

concepts.name: Parentification
concepts.note: Children assume inappropriate caregiving or adult responsibilities.

concepts.name: Enmeshment
concepts.note: Blurred relational boundaries and excessive emotional fusion.

concepts.name: Trauma bond
concepts.note: Intense attachment maintained through intermittent affection amid abuse or crisis.

concepts.name: Denial
concepts.note: Minimizing or refusing to acknowledge relational problems and harmful consequences.

concepts.name: Fear of abandonment
concepts.note: Persistent concern that relationships or caregivers will be lost.

concepts.name: Interdependence
concepts.note: Balanced mutual support preserving autonomy and individual boundaries.

methods.name: Psychotherapy
methods.note: Treatment builds self-awareness, boundaries, and healthier relational patterns.

methods.name: Twelve-step model
methods.note: Recovery approach adapted by CoDA for codependent relational patterns.

methods.name: Spann-Fischer Codependency Scale
methods.note: Self-report instrument assessing external focus and approval-seeking.

methods.name: Holyoake Codependency Index
methods.note: Instrument measuring external focus, self-sacrifice, and reactivity.

theories.name: Attachment theory
theories.note: Links codependency to insecure attachment, fear of abandonment, and clinging behavior.

theories.name: Cognitive-behavioral model
theories.note: Explains codependency through distorted beliefs connecting self-worth with relational usefulness.

theories.name: Psychoanalytic model
theories.note: Attributes codependency to trauma, unmet needs, and repetition of dysfunctional bonds.

frameworks.name: Family systems theory
frameworks.note: Treats codependency as a systemic pattern involving fusion, anxiety, and blurred boundaries.

concepts.name: Coherence
concepts.note: Mutual consistency, support, and explanatory connection among propositions.

concepts.name: Maximal coherence
concepts.note: Ideal state in which propositions form a complete mutually reinforcing system.

concepts.name: Web of belief
concepts.note: Interconnected belief structure whose overall coherence supports individual beliefs.

concepts.name: Isolation problem
concepts.note: Problem that multiple coherent systems may exist without identifying reality’s system.

concepts.name: Input problem
concepts.note: Concern that internally coherent beliefs may lack reliable connection to the world.

concepts.name: Moderate circularity
concepts.note: Holistic mutual support defended as non-vicious rather than linear justification.

principles.name: Holism
principles.note: Individual beliefs gain truth or warrant through their place in a systematic whole.

principles.name: Explanatory coherence
principles.note: Systems are favored when their propositions mutually explain evidence and experience.

methods.name: Constraint satisfaction
methods.note: Computational method assessing hypotheses by consistency and explanatory fit.

methods.name: Boat metaphor
methods.note: Neurath’s image of revising knowledge while remaining within the vessel of belief.

theories.name: Coherence theory of truth
theories.note: Defines truth by coherence within a comprehensive system of propositions.

theories.name: Coherentism
theories.note: Justifies beliefs through mutual support rather than foundational beliefs.

theories.name: Correspondence theory
theories.note: Contrasting view that truth consists in matching facts or states of affairs.

frameworks.name: Absolute idealism
frameworks.note: Treats reality and truth as an interconnected rational whole.

frameworks.name: Law as integrity
frameworks.note: Dworkin’s framework requiring legal interpretations to unify materials coherently.

concepts.name: Counterdependency
concepts.note: Defensive rejection of dependency expressed through excessive self-reliance and intimacy avoidance.

concepts.name: Hyper-independence
concepts.note: Unhealthy extreme self-reliance involving refusal of needed help.

concepts.name: Healthy emotional independence
concepts.note: Autonomy that remains open to appropriate support.

concepts.name: Fear of engulfment
concepts.note: Fear that closeness will consume autonomy or control.

concepts.name: Fear of intimacy
concepts.note: Avoidance of closeness to prevent vulnerability or rejection.

concepts.name: Internal working models
concepts.note: Attachment-based expectations about caregiver availability and personal worth.

concepts.name: Dependency continuum
concepts.note: Continuum placing codependency and counterdependency at opposing unhealthy extremes.

methods.name: Emotionally Focused Therapy
methods.note: Restructures relationship cycles and promotes responsive attachment.

methods.name: Schema therapy
methods.note: Targets maladaptive schemas underlying excessive independence.

methods.name: Role-playing
methods.note: Practices interpersonal support-seeking and vulnerability in simulated situations.

theories.name: Attachment theory
theories.note: Explains counterdependency through avoidant attachment and defensive self-reliance.

theories.name: Psychoanalytic theory
theories.note: Treats counterdependency as defense against unconscious wishes for care.

frameworks.name: Dismissive-avoidant attachment model
frameworks.note: Describes positive self-view, negative other-view, and compulsive autonomy.

frameworks.name: Interdependence model
frameworks.note: Positions healthy mutual support between codependent and counterdependent extremes.

concepts.name: Counterfactual thinking
concepts.note: Mental simulation of alternatives to events that actually occurred.

concepts.name: Upward counterfactual
concepts.note: Imagines a better outcome to motivate improvement and generate regret.

concepts.name: Downward counterfactual
concepts.note: Imagines a worse outcome to foster relief and satisfaction.

concepts.name: Additive counterfactual
concepts.note: Imagines adding an absent action or event.

concepts.name: Subtractive counterfactual
concepts.note: Imagines removing an action or event that occurred.

concepts.name: Self-referential counterfactual
concepts.note: Attributes the imagined change to one’s own actions.

concepts.name: Other-referential counterfactual
concepts.note: Attributes the imagined change to another agent’s actions.

concepts.name: Mutability
concepts.note: The ease with which an event element can be mentally altered.

concepts.name: Regret
concepts.note: Negative emotion often produced by upward comparisons with better alternatives.

principles.name: Minimality
principles.note: Counterfactuals generally alter as little of the factual scenario as possible.

principles.name: Norm violation
principles.note: Events departing from norms more readily trigger counterfactual simulation.

methods.name: Method of difference
methods.note: Mill’s causal method varies one factor to identify its counterfactual effect.

methods.name: Thought-listing protocol
methods.note: Research method recording generated counterfactual thoughts.

theories.name: Norm Theory
theories.note: Kahneman and Miller explain counterfactuals through deviations from normative scenarios.

theories.name: Functional theory
theories.note: Roese explains counterfactuals as tools for preparation and affect regulation.

theories.name: Mental models theory
theories.note: Byrne’s account constructs logically consistent alternative possibilities.

frameworks.name: Simulation heuristic
frameworks.note: Framework in which people mentally undo events to construct alternative outcomes.

coined_terms.name: Decision fatigue
coined_terms.note: Baumeister used the term for declining decision quality after extended choice.

concepts.name: Decision fatigue
concepts.note: Deterioration in decision quality and self-regulation after successive deliberations.

concepts.name: Default reliance
concepts.note: Choosing preselected options when further deliberation feels costly.

concepts.name: Choice overload
concepts.note: Burden associated with evaluating many alternatives.

concepts.name: Motivational shift
concepts.note: Alternative explanation treating fatigue as reduced willingness rather than depleted capacity.

concepts.name: Opportunity cost
concepts.note: Competing uses of time and attention influence later effort.

principles.name: Limited strength model
principles.note: Self-control draws on a finite resource that can temporarily diminish.

methods.name: Checklists
methods.note: Structured aids intended to reduce cognitive burden in repeated decisions.

methods.name: Decision aids
methods.note: Algorithms or tools intended to support consistent judgments.

methods.name: Workload distribution
methods.note: Organizational strategy distributing decisions to reduce cumulative burden.

theories.name: Ego depletion theory
theories.note: Repeated self-control acts are proposed to impair later self-regulation.

theories.name: Process-oriented model
theories.note: Apparent fatigue reflects adaptive disengagement or motivational recalibration.

coined_terms.name: Eustress
coined_terms.note: Hans Selye coined the term for beneficial, adaptive stress.

concepts.name: Eustress
concepts.note: Manageable challenge-related stress that motivates performance, growth, and adaptation.

concepts.name: Distress
concepts.note: Overwhelming or prolonged stress associated with harmful outcomes.

concepts.name: Challenge appraisal
concepts.note: Interpreting a stressor as manageable and growth-promoting.

concepts.name: Threat appraisal
concepts.note: Interpreting a stressor as exceeding coping resources.

concepts.name: Self-efficacy
concepts.note: Belief in one’s capacity to execute actions and achieve performance.

concepts.name: Flow state
concepts.note: Deep immersion arising when skills balance task challenges.

principles.name: Yerkes-Dodson law
principles.note: Moderate arousal optimizes performance, while excessive arousal impairs it.

methods.name: Goal-setting
methods.note: Uses achievable challenges to foster constructive stress and motivation.

methods.name: Mindfulness
methods.note: Presented as a technique for cultivating beneficial stress and reducing chronic distress.

methods.name: Positive reframing
methods.note: Teaches people to interpret workplace demands as beneficial challenges.

theories.name: General Adaptation Syndrome
theories.note: Selye’s model describes alarm, resistance, and exhaustion stages of stress.

theories.name: Transactional model of stress
theories.note: Lazarus and Folkman explain stress through primary and secondary appraisal.

frameworks.name: Comprehensive Hierarchical Eustress framework
frameworks.note: Identifies goal-directed, present-moment, and affiliative sources of eustress.

concepts.name: Experiential avoidance
concepts.note: Unwillingness to contact distressing private experiences and attempts to alter or escape them.

concepts.name: Psychological flexibility
concepts.note: Capacity to remain open to experience while acting according to values.

concepts.name: Cognitive fusion
concepts.note: Treating thoughts as literal truths rather than passing mental events.

concepts.name: Radical acceptance
concepts.note: Fully acknowledging painful experiences without futile escape attempts.

concepts.name: Decentering
concepts.note: Observing thoughts and feelings as transient events.

concepts.name: Negative reinforcement cycle
concepts.note: Short-term relief strengthens avoidance despite long-term harm.

principles.name: Short-term relief, long-term cost
principles.note: Avoidance reduces discomfort immediately but restricts functioning over time.

principles.name: Ironic rebound
principles.note: Suppressing unwanted thoughts can increase their later recurrence.

methods.name: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy
methods.note: Promotes contact with internal experience in service of valued action.

methods.name: Systematic desensitization
methods.note: Uses graduated exposure to counter conditioned avoidance.

methods.name: Focusing
methods.note: Attends to bodily felt experience instead of avoiding or intellectualizing it.

methods.name: Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy
methods.note: Cultivates nonjudgmental awareness of thoughts and emotions.

theories.name: Relational frame theory
theories.note: Explains how language and cognition amplify aversive private experiences.

theories.name: Ironic process theory
theories.note: Explains why deliberate thought suppression can intensify unwanted content.

theories.name: Cognitive model of panic
theories.note: Explains how avoidance and safety behaviors maintain catastrophic interpretations.

frameworks.name: ACT hexaflex
frameworks.note: Maps six processes undermining psychological flexibility and their adaptive counterparts.

concepts.name: Exposure therapy
concepts.note: Controlled confrontation with feared stimuli to reduce avoidance and fear.

concepts.name: Fear hierarchy
concepts.note: Ranked list of feared stimuli from least to most distressing.

concepts.name: Habituation
concepts.note: Decline in anxiety during sustained contact with a feared stimulus.

concepts.name: Extinction
concepts.note: Learning that a feared stimulus no longer predicts danger.

concepts.name: Inhibitory learning
concepts.note: New safety associations compete with, rather than erase, fear memories.

concepts.name: Expectancy violation
concepts.note: Exposure disconfirms predicted catastrophes and updates threat expectations.

principles.name: Avoidance maintains anxiety
principles.note: Avoidance prevents corrective learning and preserves fear responses.

principles.name: Safety behavior prevention
principles.note: Reducing rituals and safety signals strengthens exposure learning.

methods.name: In vivo exposure
methods.note: Directly confronts feared situations in real-world settings.

methods.name: Imaginal exposure
methods.note: Repeatedly recounts feared or traumatic scenarios through vivid imagery.

methods.name: Interoceptive exposure
methods.note: Induces feared bodily sensations to reduce catastrophic interpretations.

methods.name: Virtual reality exposure
methods.note: Uses simulated environments for controlled confrontation with fears.

methods.name: Systematic desensitization
methods.note: Pairs graduated exposure with relaxation to inhibit anxiety.

methods.name: Flooding
methods.note: Begins exposure immediately with the most intense feared stimulus.

methods.name: Exposure and response prevention
methods.note: Combines exposure with prevention of compulsive responses.

methods.name: Prolonged exposure therapy
methods.note: Treats PTSD through repeated imaginal and in-vivo trauma exposure.

theories.name: Inhibitory learning theory
theories.note: Explains exposure as formation of context-dependent safety memories.

theories.name: Classical conditioning
theories.note: Explains acquisition and extinction of fear through stimulus associations.

theories.name: Emotional processing theory
theories.note: Explains fear reduction through corrective information during exposure.

frameworks.name: Cognitive-behavioral therapy
frameworks.note: Therapeutic framework integrating exposure with behavioral and cognitive techniques.

concepts.name: Grit
concepts.note: Perseverance and passion directed toward long-term goals.

concepts.name: Perseverance of effort
concepts.note: Sustained effort despite obstacles, setbacks, or plateaus.

concepts.name: Consistency of interests
concepts.note: Enduring commitment to a stable set of pursuits.

concepts.name: Deliberate practice
concepts.note: Focused repeated effort that accumulates expertise.

concepts.name: Growth mindset
concepts.note: Belief that abilities can develop through effort.

concepts.name: Self-control
concepts.note: Capacity to align actions with valued goals despite temptations.

methods.name: Grit Scale
methods.note: Original twelve-item self-report measure of grit’s two facets.

methods.name: Short Grit Scale
methods.note: Eight-item measure assessing perseverance and interest consistency.

methods.name: Domain-specific Grit Scale
methods.note: Measure adapted to persistence and interests within a particular domain.

theories.name: Grit theory
theories.note: Duckworth’s account treats sustained passion and perseverance as achievement predictors.

frameworks.name: VIA Classification of Character Strengths
frameworks.note: Taxonomy placing perseverance under the virtue of courage.

concepts.name: Heteronomy
concepts.note: Condition in which will or action is determined by external laws, forces, or authorities.

concepts.name: Autonomy
concepts.note: Self-legislation of universal principles through rational agency.

concepts.name: Heteronomous morality
concepts.note: Childhood morality based on fixed externally imposed rules.

concepts.name: Moral realism
concepts.note: Early view that moral rules are objective, fixed, and authority-backed.

concepts.name: General will
concepts.note: Rousseau’s conception of citizens collectively legislating for the common good.

concepts.name: Instituted imaginary
concepts.note: Castoriadis’s socially established meanings treated as external or permanent.

principles.name: Categorical imperative
principles.note: Kant’s unconditional moral law derived from pure practical reason.

principles.name: Universal law principle
principles.note: Act only on maxims that can be willed as universal laws.

theories.name: Piaget’s theory of moral development
theories.note: Explains movement from heteronomous to autonomous moral reasoning.

theories.name: Ethics of the Other
theories.note: Levinas grounds responsibility in an externally imposed demand from another person.

frameworks.name: Kantian deontology
frameworks.note: Framework grounding moral worth in autonomous duty rather than contingent ends.

frameworks.name: Castoriadis’s social imaginary
frameworks.note: Framework contrasting autonomous self-institution with heteronomous social order.

coined_terms.name: Hormesis
coined_terms.note: Southam and Ehrlich coined the term in 1943 for low-dose stimulation by harmful agents.

concepts.name: Hormesis
concepts.note: Low stressor doses stimulate adaptive effects while high doses inhibit or harm.

concepts.name: Biphasic dose-response
concepts.note: Nonmonotonic response involving low-dose stimulation and high-dose inhibition.

concepts.name: Mithridatism
concepts.note: Gradual ingestion of sublethal poisons to cultivate tolerance.

concepts.name: Adaptive stress response
concepts.note: Protective overcompensation following mild disruption of homeostasis.

concepts.name: Mitohormesis
concepts.note: Mild mitochondrial stress induces protective and longevity-related responses.

principles.name: Dose makes the poison
principles.note: Paracelsus’s principle that effects depend on quantity rather than substance alone.

principles.name: Overcompensation
principles.note: Mild perturbation can trigger repair and protection exceeding baseline.

methods.name: Preconditioning
methods.note: Uses mild stress exposure to increase resistance to later stress.

methods.name: Caloric restriction
